title: Converting Fractions, Decimals and Percentages

findings.finding: Numerical division with remainders is used directly in the improper-to-mixed example without being rehearsed.
findings.breakdown: Students must calculate a quotient and remainder before interpreting them as wholes and leftover parts. The preceding visual grouping establishes their meaning but does not rehearse this numerical calculation.
findings.checked: p7-teaching and p7-guided-practice use drawn groups. p12-rule and p12-guided practise multiplication and addition. p13-example-demonstration supplies the result of 11 ÷ 4.
findings.assumptions: Division with remainders is prior knowledge. No calculator is assumed.

repair.proposal: At the opening of the rule-based conversion topic, add: 'Write the whole-number quotient and remainder: (a) 8 ÷ 3; (b) 17 ÷ 5; (c) 20 ÷ 4. Check using divisor × quotient + remainder.' Answers: 2 remainder 2; 3 remainder 2; 5 remainder 0.

findings.doneWhen: The review rehearses numerical quotient-and-remainder calculation before the improper-to-mixed example.

findings.finding: The unchanged independent task of converting 2 1/5 to an improper fraction occurs twice.
findings.breakdown: Both copies have the same value, conversion requirement and absence of scaffolding. No retrieval or comparison purpose connects the copies.
findings.checked: Compared both complete parts and their parent instructions. p15-q4-a–c deliberately varies the whole-number part, so its middle member should remain.
findings.assumptions: The exercise is assigned as presented.

repair.proposal: Remove p14-q1-d and retain p15-q4-b to preserve the whole-part variation in p15-q4-a–c.

findings.doneWhen: The task occurs once and the existing variation group remains intact.

findings.finding: The rational-number examples use percentage meaning and decimal place-value conversion without rehearsing those general conversion steps.
findings.breakdown: Recognising why 47% becomes 47/100 and why 0.125 becomes 125/1000 is necessary to follow the integer-fraction criterion. Remembered common equivalents do not rehearse choosing these numerators and denominators.
findings.checked: p18-common-fdp and p19-q1 rehearse particular common equivalents. Earlier mixed-number topics do not rehearse either general conversion.
findings.assumptions: Basic percentage meaning and decimal place value are prior learning. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before p20-information, add: 'Write as fractions with denominator 100: (a) 23%; (b) 7%. Write as fractions with denominator 10, 100 or 1000: (c) 0.6; (d) 0.037.' Answers: 23/100, 7/100, 6/10, 37/1000. Do not require simplification.

findings.doneWhen: Both representation decisions are rehearsed before they support the definition of rationality.

findings.finding: The opening review omits simplifying and scaling equivalent fractions, both direct steps in the worked conversions.
findings.breakdown: Choosing a place-value denominator does not rebuild the skill of changing numerator and denominator together. Students need that skill to follow both the simplification examples and the construction of tenths or hundredths.
findings.checked: p21-q1 and p21-q2 rehearse place-value representations only. p20-q4 requires integer-fraction representations but does not require simplification or scaling an existing fraction.
findings.assumptions: Equivalent fractions and simplification are prior knowledge. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Add: 'Find the missing numerator: 3/5 = □/10; 7/20 = □/100. Simplify: 6/10; 15/100.' Answers: 6, 35, 3/5, 3/20. Keep these short items within the existing review page.

findings.doneWhen: The review rehearses equal multiplication and division of numerator and denominator before the examples use them.

findings.finding: Recurring-decimal practice requires marking non-recurring prefixes and complete repeating blocks before these notation variants are explained.
findings.breakdown: Students who have encountered only a dotted single digit may include a non-recurring digit in the repetition, mark only the last digit of a repeating block, or copy a rounded calculator display as exact.
findings.checked: p18-common-fdp supplies single-digit notation without an explanation. p20-information supplies an expanded recurring decimal. p23-teaching covers power-of-ten equivalents. p25-q8 gives calculator access but no notation model. p27-q1-c later explains display approximation, and p27-q2-a later models single-digit notation; neither supplies the missing block and prefix models before p25-q8.
findings.assumptions: A calculator is explicitly available for p25-q8. The finding concerns notation and exactness, not calculator arithmetic.

repair.proposal: Before p25-q8, add: 'Divide the numerator by the denominator. Mark only the digits that repeat indefinitely; the calculator displays finitely many digits and may round the last one.' Model 5 ÷ 6 = 0.83333… = 0.8\dot{3}, explaining that the 8 does not repeat, and 8 ÷ 11 = 0.727272… = 0.\overline{72}, explaining that the bar covers the complete repeating block.

findings.doneWhen: One explanation before p25-q8 supplies the notation needed by both topics, including prefixes, repeating blocks and finite calculator displays.

findings.finding: The exact conversion of recurring decimals with non-recurring prefixes is required without a preceding model of that variant.
findings.breakdown: The patterns established over 9, 99 and 999 apply when repetition begins immediately after the decimal point. They do not directly explain how to scale a recurring tail or combine it with a non-recurring prefix.
findings.checked: p28-q3 through p28-q5 teach purely recurring conversions through patterns. p22-teaching covers terminating decimals. p27-q2-g converts in the opposite direction. The deliberate contrasts within p29-q6 do not themselves state the missing conversion route.
findings.assumptions: Basic fraction arithmetic and decimal scaling are prior knowledge. Calculator access does not supply the exact-conversion reasoning.

repair.proposal: Before p29-q6-f, model: '0.0\dot{4} = 0.\dot{4} ÷ 10 = (4/9) ÷ 10 = 4/90 = 2/45. Then 0.1\dot{4} = 1/10 + 4/90 = 13/90. Each further shift right divides by another 10. Keep any whole-number part separately.' Retain the existing question order and contrasts.

findings.doneWhen: Students have seen both scaling a recurring tail and combining it with a non-recurring prefix before attempting the variants.

findings.finding: The decimal-percentage example skips the connecting step that clears a decimal numerator.
findings.breakdown: The jump from 10.5/100 to 21/200 hides the decision to change both numerator and denominator when making the numerator an integer.
findings.checked: p22-teaching starts with a decimal value and a place-value denominator. p23-teaching uses integer fractions. The preceding percentage examples simplify integer numerators; none models clearing a decimal numerator.
findings.assumptions: Students know ordinary equivalent fractions and integer simplification. No calculator is assumed.

repair.proposal: Insert: 'Multiply numerator and denominator by 10 to make the numerator an integer, then simplify.' Show 10.5/100 = 105/1000 = 21/200.

findings.doneWhen: The example explicitly shows equal scaling before simplification.

findings.finding: The score 28 out of 30 requires a fraction-to-percentage route beyond the integer-hundredths method taught so far.
findings.breakdown: The reduced denominator 15 cannot become 100 by integer scaling. Students have encountered recurring decimals, but have not yet been taught the general decimal-to-percentage step needed for this route.
findings.checked: p32-q2, p33-q3 and p34-q5 use equivalent fractions suited to hundredths. p18-common-fdp supplies the memorised percentage for 1/3. The general numerator-division and decimal × 100 route appears later in p37-conversion-diagram.
findings.assumptions: A general fraction-to-percentage method has not been taught separately. The repair can use short division or a calculator.

repair.proposal: Before p35-q12-response, add: 'Another route is to divide the numerator by the denominator, then multiply the decimal by 100 to obtain the percentage. For example, 2/3 = 0.666… = 66.666…% = 66.\dot{6}%. The final 6 repeats indefinitely.'

findings.doneWhen: Students have a model of converting a fraction to a recurring percentage before attempting 28/30.

findings.finding: The first dissection moves sharply from counting supplied equal-area parts to constructing and combining area units.
findings.breakdown: Students must now choose helper subdivisions, distinguish unequal labelled regions from equal units, and combine or subtract areas before converting them. These decisions appear together without a bridge.
findings.checked: p41-q4 and p41-q5 supply equal-area partitions. Earlier visual conversion teaching does likewise. p41-q6 supplies comparisons rather than area decomposition. No preceding question bridges the decomposition demand.
findings.assumptions: Rectangle and triangle area reasoning is prior knowledge, consistent with the separate area booklets. Calculator use does not resolve the decomposition decision.

repair.proposal: Before the first dissection, add: 'Try extending existing boundaries to split regions into rectangles and triangles. A diagonal divides a rectangle into two equal-area triangles. Find a labelled region by combining these smaller areas or subtracting known areas from a larger region, then compare it with the whole square.'

findings.doneWhen: Students have a route into area decomposition while still determining each region's fraction and percentage themselves.

findings.finding: Classification requires rules for non-square integer roots and rational transformations of irrational numbers that the teaching does not supply.
findings.breakdown: The definitions and isolated examples do not give students a valid way to classify unfamiliar roots or expressions such as √5 + 1 and √2/2. The identification prompt correctly excludes treating a finite calculator display as proof.
findings.checked: p43-rational-vs-irrational names π and √2. p43-real-number-diagram-block gives particular examples. Earlier topics teach rational representations. p44-key-ideas restates decimal criteria without adding root or transformation rules.
findings.assumptions: These classification rules are new in this introductory irrational-number sequence. Calculator evaluation of roots is available but cannot establish irrationality.

repair.proposal: Before p44-identify, add: 'For a positive integer n, √n is rational if n is a perfect square and irrational otherwise. For example, √9 = 3 is rational; √5 is irrational. Adding a rational number to an irrational number, or multiplying or dividing an irrational number by a nonzero rational number, gives an irrational number. Thus √5 + 1, 2√2 and √2/2 are irrational. Use the original expressions to decide, rather than the calculator display.'

findings.doneWhen: The classification criteria are stated before unfamiliar roots and rational transformations are classified.

findings.finding: The opening review rehearses decimal ordering but omits the two conversion routes used directly by the ordering example.
findings.breakdown: Students must first convert fractions and percentages to decimals. The example supplies the results, so the review does not reveal whether students can independently perform this first stage.
findings.checked: p49-q1 and p49-q2 contain decimals only. Both routes were taught earlier. The immediately preceding irrational-number topic contains isolated conversions, rather than a review or sustained exercise of both routes.
findings.assumptions: Previously taught conversion methods require recall before being combined with ordering. Calculator use is available; choosing the conversion route remains necessary.

repair.proposal: Add: 'Write each as a decimal: (a) 1/5; (b) 3/4; (c) 4/8; (d) 18%; (e) 75%; (f) 8%.' Answers: 0.2, 0.75, 0.5, 0.18, 0.75, 0.08. Keep this short item with the existing review.

findings.doneWhen: The opening review checks both conversions before students combine them with ordering.

findings.finding: Generalise regrouping between whole units and fractional pieces while preserving a fixed value.
findings.breakdown: The task explains the existing p17-q12-e–h comparison and distinguishes regrouped sums from standard mixed numerals.
findings.checked: The rule-based conversions and the definition of a proper fractional part supply the required methods. For integer k from 0 to 5, 7k + (39 − 7k) = 39; only k = 5 leaves a proper fractional part.
findings.assumptions: An optional generalisation may use a letter to describe a whole-number choice.

repair.proposal: After p17-q12-h, offer: 'Starting with 39/7 = 5 + 4/7, explain how to reduce the whole part by one without changing the value. Write a sum using any whole-number part k from 0 to 5. Which is a standard mixed numeral?' Expected answer: removing a whole adds 7 to the numerator; 39/7 = k + (39 − 7k)/7. Only k = 5 gives the standard mixed numeral 5 4/7.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task connects the existing regrouping pattern to a general expression.

findings.finding: Explain why repeating blocks of different lengths can describe the same decimal.
findings.breakdown: Students connect the denominator patterns with equivalent fractions and distinguish a repeating block from its shortest description.
findings.checked: The patterns over 9, 99 and 999 are established in p28-q3–q5. The equalities 4/9 = 44/99 = 444/999 and 23/99 = 2323/9999 are correct.
findings.assumptions: Equivalent-fraction arithmetic is available by the end of the topic.

repair.proposal: After p29-q6, offer: 'Predict whether 0.\dot{4}, 0.\overline{44} and 0.\overline{444} are equal. Convert each to a fraction to explain. Then give two repeating-block descriptions of 0.\overline{23} and explain their equality.' Expected answer: 4/9 = 44/99 = 444/999; for example, 0.\overline{23} = 0.\overline{2323}, since multiplying 23/99 by 101/101 gives 2323/9999.

findings.doneWhen: Students explain equivalent repeating-block descriptions using the taught fraction patterns.

findings.finding: Find which whole-number percentages correspond to an exact count out of 25.
findings.breakdown: Students generalise the equivalent-fraction structure already used to find counts from percentages.
findings.checked: p36-q16 supplies the denominator-change method and p36-q17 applies it to 25. For an integer percentage p between 0 and 100, the count is p/4, which is an integer exactly when p is divisible by 4.
findings.assumptions: The question concerns exact counts in a class of 25.

repair.proposal: After p36-q18-response, offer: 'A class has 25 students. Which whole-number percentages from 0% to 100% can describe an exact number of students? Explain using equivalent fractions.' Expected answer: 0%, 4%, 8%, …, 100%, because p/100 = (p/4)/25 and the count must be a whole number.

findings.doneWhen: Students explain the multiples-of-four condition through equivalent fractions.

findings.finding: Compare a fixed recurring fraction with successively longer terminating approximations.
findings.breakdown: The run exposes why additional matching digits bring values closer without making a finite decimal equal to the recurring value.
findings.checked: Recurring notation and decimal ordering have been taught. Every listed terminating decimal is less than 2/3; the follow-up order is 66.6% < 2/3 < 0.667. No supplied run varies only the number of terminating sixes.
findings.assumptions: Students compare exact recurring values rather than rounded calculator displays.

repair.proposal: After p51-q1-h, add: 'Predict whether each value is smaller than, equal to or greater than 2/3. Insert <, = or >: 0.6 __ 2/3; 0.66 __ 2/3; 0.666 __ 2/3; 0.6666 __ 2/3. What changes, and why does equality never occur?' Answers: all <; the terminating string grows, but 2/3 has further sixes indefinitely. Keep 2/3 fixed and vary only the number of terminating sixes. Follow with: 'Order 0.667, 66.6%, 2/3 in ascending order.' Answer: 66.6%, 2/3, 0.667.

findings.doneWhen: The run includes prediction, explanation and an unpatterned comparison using the same distinction.

protectedGroups.observation: A fraction changes from proper to improper when its denominator crosses below its numerator.
The same set separates into values below, equal to and above one; equality is distinct from strict inequality.
Moving the pointer changes the fractional part while preserving the whole part and denominator.
protectedGroups.invariant: Integer labels, eighth-unit intervals and whole part one.

protectedGroups.observation: Moving one interval right increases the mixed number by one fifth.
protectedGroups.invariant: Integer labels, fifth-unit intervals and whole part two.

protectedGroups.observation: Conversion includes exact whole quantities with no leftover fractional part.
protectedGroups.varies: Conversion direction, denominator and whole count.
protectedGroups.invariant: All shaded parts form complete wholes.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing the part size and part count together can preserve the same number of wholes.
Each additional whole contributes five fifths.
Fractional positions remain readable as labels and the visible zero are progressively removed.
protectedGroups.varies: Label support, denominator and visible starting value.
protectedGroups.invariant: Equal intervals within a labelled unit determine the fraction size.

protectedGroups.observation: Increasing the whole part by one adds five to the improper numerator.
Increasing the fractional numerator by one increases the improper numerator by one.
The denominator determines how many fractional pieces each whole contributes.
Doubling the improper numerator doubles the represented quantity, with regrouping and possible simplification.
Halving the denominator doubles the represented quantity and can remove the fractional remainder.
Removing one whole requires adding seven sevenths to preserve the value.
protectedGroups.varies: Whole part decreases by one and the missing numerator increases by seven.

protectedGroups.observation: The growing decimal prefix exposes how the number of decimal places determines a power-of-ten denominator.
protectedGroups.varies: The number of decimal places increases from one to two to three.
protectedGroups.invariant: Each value is a positive terminating decimal beginning with 0.4, and each task asks for an integer fraction representation.

protectedGroups.observation: The same numerator represents a value ten times smaller at each step.
Moving the decimal point one place left multiplies the required denominator by 10.
protectedGroups.varies: Decimal position and number of decimal places.

protectedGroups.observation: Unit fractions decrease as the denominator increases, whether their decimals terminate or recur.
The recurring digit matches the numerator of a proper fraction with denominator nine, allowing students to reverse the relationship.
protectedGroups.invariant: Denominator nine and a single repeating digit.

protectedGroups.observation: Denominator 99 produces a two-digit repeating block, including a leading zero when needed.
protectedGroups.invariant: Denominator 99 and two positions in the repeating block.

protectedGroups.observation: Denominator 999 produces a three-digit repeating block; leading zeroes count as positions.
protectedGroups.varies: Numerator and number of leading zeroes, then direction of conversion.
protectedGroups.invariant: Denominator 999 and three positions in the repeating block.

protectedGroups.observation: Moving or preceding the same recurring digit changes the value and its fraction representation; preserve this contrast after adding the missing teaching.
protectedGroups.varies: Position of recurrence and the non-recurring prefix.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing the whole part preserves the fractional part, whereas inserting a non-recurring zero scales the recurring fractional part.
protectedGroups.varies: First the whole part, then the position at which recurrence begins.

protectedGroups.observation: Increasing the numerator by one fifth increases the decimal by 0.2.
Scaling only the denominator changes the value; scaling numerator and denominator together preserves it.
protectedGroups.varies: Denominator scaling, followed by joint numerator–denominator scaling.

protectedGroups.observation: Internal zeroes change the fractional place value without changing the whole-number part.
protectedGroups.varies: Position of the digit 5 after the decimal point.

protectedGroups.observation: Selected consecutive runs expose tenfold place-value changes and the irrelevance of trailing decimal zeroes.
protectedGroups.invariant: The conversion factor of 100 within each column.

protectedGroups.observation: Decimal conversion preserves place value, including trailing-zero removal and insertion of a leading zero.
protectedGroups.varies: The percentage changes from 82 to 80 to 8.
protectedGroups.invariant: Every percentage number is divided by 100.

protectedGroups.observation: Both inputs can be rewritten in quarters before conversion to hundredths.
protectedGroups.invariant: The supplied intermediate denominator is 4, followed by denominator 100.

protectedGroups.observation: An integer, a terminating decimal and a recurring decimal can all be rational.
A square root can be rational or irrational, and adding 1 to the irrational example preserves irrationality.
protectedGroups.varies: Radicand, then addition of an integer.
protectedGroups.invariant: Square-root structure; parts j and k retain the same irrational component.

protectedGroups.observation: Doubling √6 changes its value, while rewriting 2√6 as √24 preserves its value and location.
protectedGroups.invariant: Classification and response format; rows 03 and 04 have the same exact value.

droppedQuestions.question: Have students already learned that a dot marks a digit repeating indefinitely, including how to read 0.\dot{3} and 33.\dot{3}%? If not, these entries need a brief explanation before students memorise them.
droppedQuestions.reason: Knowing whether students already understand a single dotted digit would not resolve the retained finding about multi-digit repeating blocks and non-recurring prefixes. p27-q2-a explicitly pairs expanded single-digit recurrence with dot notation; this question would principally support a new finding about the earlier table, which this review is not authorised to add.
